title: WorldEdit: Open-World Image Editing with Causal Knowledge
one_liner: A dataset and training method that teaches image editors to understand implicit editing instructions by grounding them in real-world cause-and-effect logic.
lead: Image editing models today are good at following direct orders like 'make it red' or 'add sunglasses'. But they fail when you say 'this metal will rust after rain' — a cause-and-effect instruction that requires understanding how the real world works. WorldEdit fixes this by providing a dataset of real-world causal edits paired with instructions, then fine-tuning models with a special reward signal that checks whether the edit actually follows the rules of physics and common sense.

paras: Image editing models today are trained on pairs of images and simple, direct instructions: 'add glasses', 'change the color to blue', 'rotate the person'. These explicit instructions work well because they say exactly what the output should look like.

But real-world edits often describe a cause, not an outcome. 'This metal will rust in the rain' does not say what color to paint or where to put the rust — it just names a cause. The model has to know that rust is reddish-brown, spreads on exposed steel, and appears where water collects. A beginner model trained only on 'make it blue' has no notion that rain causes rust, or where rust lives on metal, or what it looks like in this exact photo.

Existing training data does not teach this. The model sees a picture and a label, but nobody told it that the label 'rust forms on steel in rain' is a causal rule you can apply to new images, not just a tag to memorize.

callout.html: Models fail on implicit instructions because they have never learned the causal rules of the real world embedded in the data they work with.

steps.text: Take real images, identify objects in them, and ask: what changes under different conditions? Use an LLM to answer and generate paraphrased instructions grounded in real-world logic.
Use GPT-4o to apply the causal edits to the originals — if a single step fails, break the instruction into smaller steps until the edit works and looks real.
Train the model (Bagel) on pairs of original image, implicit instruction, and edited image, teaching it to map causal language to visual changes.
Use reinforcement learning to fine-tune the model further, rewarding it when edits are causally correct, visually realistic, and faithful to the instruction.
Test on WorldEdit-Test, a separate set of causal edits, and compare reasoning quality and world knowledge against open-source and closed models.

paras: The paper changes two things: the training data (a dataset pairing real images with causal instructions) and the training signal (a multi-part reward that checks whether edits obey world knowledge). Instead of training on generic image-edit pairs, WorldEdit trains on cause-and-effect scenarios where the instruction names a physical or logical cause, and the model learns to produce edits that honor real-world rules.

hidden.h2: Causal coherence: does the edit obey world rules?
hidden.name: Causal coherence score
paras: The hidden quantity is causal coherence — a measure of whether the edited image follows real-world cause-and-effect logic. When you say 'rust forms on steel after rain', the edit should show rust in the places where rain would collect and where steel is exposed. The edit should not show rust on paint, or appear in places where water does not reach. Causal coherence is not whether the instruction was followed literally — it is whether the edit is plausible in the real world.

The paper estimates this by building a multi-part reward: one part checks that the instruction was understood correctly (reasoning reward), one part checks that the image quality is high and photorealistic (fidelity reward), and one part checks that the edit obeys real-world cause-and-effect relationships (causal verification reward). Only edits that score well on all three are rewarded during training.

heat.caption: Darker means causal correctness: rust on steel (dark), not on paint (light), missing from protected areas (light).

reads.html: Causal coherence is whether an edit follows the rules of the real world. If the instruction is 'rust forms in rain', the edit should show rust where rain touches steel, not where paint covers it. The model learns to produce edits that pass this common-sense test.

The causal verification reward component specifically scores whether the generated image respects real-world cause-and-effect relationships embedded in the instruction. This guides the model away from arbitrary edits toward edits that are both visually plausible and causally grounded. It is one of three reward signals (reasoning, fidelity, and causal correctness) combined to guide training.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: from implicit instructions to causal edits
paras: The mechanism has three parts. First, the dataset teaches the model what causal instructions sound like and how they map to visual changes. Instead of seeing 'add sunglasses' paired with an image wearing sunglasses, the model sees 'these sunglasses would fog up if the person walked from a warm room into cold air' paired with an image showing frosted lenses. The instruction is richer and encodes real-world knowledge.

Second, supervised fine-tuning on this dataset lets the model learn to decode implicit instructions. When it sees 'this metal will rust after rain', it can now predict what the edited image should show, because it has learned patterns from similar causal scenarios in the dataset.

Third, the reinforcement learning stage with the causal reward signal fine-tunes this knowledge. The model generates multiple candidate edits. The ones that are causally correct (e.g., rust appears where water collects), visually realistic, and faithful to the instruction are rewarded. The ones that are causally wrong (e.g., rust appears on paint, or in dry areas) are penalized. Over training, the model learns to avoid causally implausible edits and converges on edits that pass all three tests: they are well-reasoned, visually good, and causally sound.

Model decodes instruction into visual plan

math.h2: The reward function: three signals in balance
math.words: Total reward equals reasoning reward plus fidelity reward plus causal reward. Each component scores a different aspect. The model learns to maximize the total.
symbols: Total reward score for an edit candidate
How well the model understood and reasoned about the instruction
How visually realistic and high-quality the edited image is
How well the edit obeys real-world cause-and-effect logic

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Instruction: 'This leather will age and crack over 10 years exposed to sun.'
Candidate edit 1: Shows leather darkened and cracked in exposed areas. R_reason = 8 (good understanding). R_fidelity = 9 (photorealistic). R_causal = 9 (cracks appear where sun hits). Total = 26.

Candidate edit 2: Shows leather smooth but uniformly faded everywhere. R_reason = 6 (partial). R_fidelity = 7 (slightly artificial). R_causal = 3 (fading without cracking is not causally coherent). Total = 16.
The model learns to favor candidate 1 (higher total reward) and avoid candidate 2.

math.note: The three-part reward teaches the model to balance understanding the instruction, making a realistic image, and obeying real-world cause-and-effect — all three matter equally.

bars.h2: The improvement: from poor implicit understanding to causal mastery

charts.title: Baseline (Bagel without WorldEdit)
charts.note: Model excels at explicit orders but fails on implicit, causal reasoning.

charts.title: WorldEdit fine-tuned model
charts.note: Training on causal data and reinforcing with causal rewards bridges the gap. Implicit and causal understanding now rival explicit performance.

items.html: Instructions like 'a person gets sunburned, then peels, then tans over weeks' require multiple sequential edits and temporal reasoning. The model can confuse the order or miss intermediate steps.

Some edits require precise understanding of physics. For example, 'a Möbius strip rotated' or 'collapsed building blocks scattered' — these require spatial and structural reasoning that even large models struggle with.
If the training data contains few examples of a causal scenario (e.g., 'rare mineral oxidation' or 'ancient ink fading'), the model will not learn it well and may produce implausible edits.

When training data is rich, the instructions are clearly paraphrased, and the causal reward is calibrated well, the model learns to produce edits that are both visually good and causally sound across a wide range of real-world scenarios.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A runnable demo should take a set of images and a set of implicit, causal instructions — for example, 'this fabric will shrink if washed in hot water', 'this metal will oxidize in humid conditions', 'this wooden frame will warp in dry heat'. For each image-instruction pair, generate an edit and evaluate it on three fronts: Did the model understand the instruction correctly? Is the edit visually realistic? Does the edit obey real-world cause-and-effect logic? Compare scores against a baseline model trained without WorldEdit.
demo.metric_eq: Overall score = (understanding + fidelity + causal correctness) / 3. Compare WorldEdit-trained model vs baseline.
demo.closing: The demo must make it impossible to miss that the WorldEdit-trained model understands implicit, causal instructions and produces edits that follow real-world logic — not just any plausible image, but one that is physically and logically coherent.
